newsitem.title: USA: U.S. coffee consumption stable in early '97 - NCA.
newsitem.headline: U.S. coffee consumption stable in early '97 - NCA.

text.p: U.S. coffee consumption appeared modestly lower but stable in early 1997, abating a long period of decline, according to a study by the National Coffee Association.

The NCA randomly surveyed 3,300 consumers aged 10 and over throughout the U.S. in January and February of 1997. While the results of the annual Winter Coffee Study will not be available until late March, delegates to the NCA's annual convention here were offered an early glimpse of the data.

It found that U.S. consumers drank an average of 1.60 cups per day during the first two months of 1997, down slightly from 1.69 cups a year ago and 1.67 cups in 1995. By comparison, Americans consumed more than three cups daily in 1960.
The number of Americans drinking coffee fell modestly in the latest survey, with 48.6 percent of U.S. consumers identifying themselves as coffee drinkers compared with 49.3 percent last year.
The United States is the world's leading consumer of coffee.
Although the latest consumption figures are still far below 1960 levels, when U.S. coffee drinking was at its peak, industry members were encouraged by this year's data.
"The consumption is stable following years of decline" Ed Marra, president of Nestle U.S.A.'s Beverage Division, said in a presentation.
"In younger consumers the decline is abating, speciality coffee consumption is inching up, consumers perceive coffee drinking is on an uptrend and consumption in the West is the highest since 1989."
Relaxed health concerns and the perception that coffee is an affordable luxury also lent support to the industry, Marra said.
Marra said the industry could attract more consumers by adding value to coffee, maintaining a consistant high quality and approaching marketing with a fresh way.
"The key issue is new eyes," he said. "Don't confine coffee to a certain market that is marketed in a certain way."

But while industry executives remained upbeat, the mood was tempered by concerns that a continued uptrend in futures prices could translate into further price hikes on the supermarket shelf which could in turn depress consumption.

Since the beginning of the year, futures prices on the Coffee, Sugar and Cocoa Exchange in New York have jumped some 50 percent, prompting roasters to raise the price of their regular 13-ounce can of ground coffee by 20 percent.

Sharp increases in futures following two severe frosts in Brazil led to huge 71 percent increase in a regular can of coffee during the second half of 1994 and contributed to the decline in coffee consumption.
